ican: I can state what a light-year is.
I can change a distance in light-years into metres with d = vt.
I can change a distance in metres into light-years.
I can explain why we see a star as it was in the past.

cloze.title: Say it the exam way
cloze.text:
A light-year is the [[distance|time]] light travels in one [[year|second]]. Light travels at [[3.0 × 10⁸|3.0 × 10⁶]] m s⁻¹.

To change light-years into metres, use [[d = vt|v = fλ]]. Put the time in [[seconds|years]]. One year is 365.25 × 24 × 60 × 60 s.

A star is 640 light-years away. Its light takes [[640 years|640 seconds]] to reach us. We see the star as it was in the [[past|present]].

mc.alt: A student makes the following statements about the Universe. I: one light-year is the time taken for light to travel from the Sun to the Earth. II: the approximate age of the Universe is 13.8 billion years. III: the 'Big Bang' theory describes the origin of the Universe. Which of these statements is or are correct? A II only, B III only, C I and III only, D II and III only, E I, II and III.
fb: Not this one. II is right, but III is right too: the Big Bang theory describes the origin of the Universe.
Not this one. III is right, but so is II: the Universe is about 13.8 billion years old.
Not this one. I is wrong. A light-year is a distance: how far light travels in one year.
Right. II and III are true. I is wrong: a light-year is the distance light travels in one year, not a time.
Not this one. I is wrong. A light-year is a distance, not a time.

mc.alt: A pulse of light from a laser is transmitted from the Earth to the Moon. The light reflects from a mirror on the Moon and is detected back on Earth 2.6 s after being transmitted. The distance from the Earth to the Moon is: A 8.8 times 10 squared m, B 1.2 times 10 to the 8 m, C 2.3 times 10 to the 8 m, D 3.9 times 10 to the 8 m, E 7.8 times 10 to the 8 m.
fb: Not this one. This uses the speed of sound (340 m s<sup>−1</sup>). Laser light travels at 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>.
Not this one. This divides the speed by the time. Use <var>d</var> = <var>vt</var>: multiply.
Not this one. This divides the speed by half the time. Use <var>d</var> = <var>vt</var>: multiply 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> by 1.3 s.
Right. The light goes there and back, so the time one way is 1.3 s. d = vt = 3.0 × 108 × 1.3 = 3.9 × 108 m.
Not this one. 7.8 × 10<sup>8</sup> m is the distance there and back. Halve the time first.

p2_tip: Set every calculation out with IESSUU. Write <var>d</var> = <var>vt</var> first, every time: “Many candidates omitted to include a correct relationship in their response” (2023 Course Report). The speed of light is on the data sheet given in each exam paper.

paper2.alt: Launched in 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is the world's premier space-based science observatory. The NASA website states that the JWST will solve mysteries in our Solar System and probe the mysterious structures and origins of our Universe. (b) In 2023, the JWST was used to study the exoplanet LHS 475 b. (ii) LHS 475 b orbits a star in the constellation Octans. The star is 41 light-years from Earth. Determine the distance, in metres, from this star to Earth. 3 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2024 Question 6(b)(ii). d = vt (1). d = 3.0 times 10 to the 8, times (41 times 365.25 times 24 times 60 times 60) (1). d = 3.9 times 10 to the 17 m (1). Not a standard three marker: the calculation can be done in steps, but all steps must be shown for the substitution mark. Accept 4 times 10 to the 17, 3.88 times 10 to the 17, 3.882 times 10 to the 17; also, using 365 days, 3.879 times 10 to the 17.

paper2.lead: Parts (a) and (b)(i) belong to other lessons.

paper2.alt: An astronomer is using a space-based telescope to observe a star. (c) The star is 343 light-years from Earth. Show that the distance from the star to Earth is 3.2 times 10 to the 18 m. 2 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2023 Question 5(c). A 'show' question. d = vt (1). d = 3.0 times 10 to the 8, times (343 times 365.25 times 24 times 60 times 60) (1). d = 3.2 times 10 to the 18 m. The final answer of 3.2 times 10 to the 18 m, including unit, must be shown or MAX (1). Accept use of d = st if it is made clear. Accept use of 365 days.

paper2.lead: Parts (a) and (b) belong to other lessons.

paper2.alt: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. Making plans for Rigel. Betelgeuse might be regularly mentioned in the news but there are other supergiants in the night sky. One of these is Rigel, a blue supergiant star that makes up the 'left foot' of the constellation of Orion. It is approximately 8 million years old and is one of the brightest stars in our night sky. A picture of Orion marks Betelgeuse and Rigel. Blue supergiants, such as Rigel, are short-lived and are destined to explode as a supernova. Even though Rigel is 860 light-years from Earth, the supernova will be clear to see. Astronomers believe that it will be as bright as a half-moon and will be visible in the sky during the day. However, the light show will only last a few months before it fades. When it explodes, Rigel will throw debris into space at approximately 5% of the speed of light. Intense waves of radiation, including X-rays and gamma rays, will be radiated into space. The core of the star will collapse into an extremely dense ball of nuclear matter called a neutron star. It is not possible to predict exactly when Rigel will explode and there is the possibility that it has already happened, it just hasn't been detected yet! The best estimate scientists have is that it will take place within the next million years, or so. (a)(i) Calculate the distance, in metres, from Rigel to Earth. 3 marks. (ii) Determine the approximate speed of the debris that will be ejected from the star during the supernova explosion. 1 mark. (iii) Calculate the time it would take for this debris to reach Earth. 3 marks. (b) Explain why the supernova explosion may already have happened but has not yet been detected. 1 mark.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2022 Question 5. (a)(i) d = vt (1), d = 3.0 times 10 to the 8, times (860 times 365.25 times 24 times 60 times 60) (1), d = 8.1 times 10 to the 18 m (1). Not a standard three marker. Accept 8 times 10 to the 18, 8.14 times 10 to the 18, 8.142 times 10 to the 18; with 365 days 8.136 times 10 to the 18. (a)(ii) v = 5 over 100 times 3.0 times 10 to the 8 = 1.5 times 10 to the 7 metres per second (1). (a)(iii) d = vt (1), 8.1 times 10 to the 18 = 1.5 times 10 to the 7 times t (1), t = 5.4 times 10 to the 11 s (1). (b) Light or EM radiation will take 860 years to reach Earth, or the light from the supernova has not reached Earth yet (1). Do not accept an explanation in terms of distance alone.

paper2.alt: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. Supernova explosion. A photograph shows a bright exploding star. The average temperature of the surface of the Sun is 5778 K. In the core of the Sun energy is produced by nuclear fusion. Once the Sun has used all its nuclear fuel it will collapse to form a white dwarf. A star with a mass much larger than that of the Sun will end its life in an enormous explosion called a supernova. The energy released in a supernova explosion is more than a hundred times the energy that the Sun will radiate over its entire 10 billion year lifetime. In our galaxy, the star Betelgeuse is predicted to explode in a supernova. Betelgeuse has a mass of around 8 times the mass of the Sun. Even though Betelgeuse is 640 light-years from Earth, the supernova will be as bright as a full moon at night in our sky. (c) Show that the distance from Earth to Betelgeuse is 6.1 times 10 to the 18 m. 3 marks. (d) Betelgeuse may have already exploded in a supernova. Explain this statement. 1 mark.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2016 Question 13. (c) A 'show that' question: must start with the correct equation or MAX (1) for the speed of light. d = vt (1). d = 3.0 times 10 to the 8, times (365.25 times 24 times 60 times 60 times 640) (1). d = 6.1 times 10 to the 18 m. One mark for the initial equation, one for the speed of light from the data sheet, one for substituting all parts of the time. (d) The light or radiation from the explosion has not reached the Earth yet, or it takes 640 years to reach Earth (1). Do not accept an explanation in terms of distance rather than time, for example 'it's 640 light-years away' alone.

paper2.lead: Parts (a) and (b) are about the Sun, so they are left out.

paper2.alt: (b) The star is 97 light-years from Earth. (i) State what is meant by the term light-year. 1 mark.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2019 Question 4(b)(i). 1 mark: the distance light travels in one year.

paper2.alt: The star Wolf 359 is at a distance of 7.8 light-years from Earth. A radio signal from Wolf 359 is detected by a radio telescope on Earth. A photograph shows a radio telescope dish. (a)(i) State the speed of the radio waves. 1 mark. (ii) Calculate the distance, in metres, from Wolf 359 to Earth. 3 marks. (b) Another telescope is used to observe the same star in the visible part of the spectrum. (i) State a suitable detector of visible light that may be used in this telescope. 1 mark. (ii) State whether the time taken for the visible light from the star to reach Earth is less than, equal to, or greater than the time taken for the radio waves from the star to reach Earth. 1 mark.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2017 Question 12. (a)(i) 3.0 times 10 to the 8 metres per second (1). (a)(ii) d = vt (1), d = 3.0 times 10 to the 8, times (7.8 times 365.25 times 24 times 60 times 60) (1), d = 7.4 times 10 to the 16 m (1); accept 7 times 10 to the 16, 7.38 times 10 to the 16, 7.384 times 10 to the 16, or with 365 days 7.379 times 10 to the 16. (b)(i) photographic film (1); accept charge coupled device or CCD, photodiode, phototransistor, retina, LDR. (b)(ii) equal (to) (1).

paper2.ref: Our question: metres to light-years (not from an exam paper)
paper2.text:
Altair is 1.58 × 1017 m from Earth.

Calculate this distance in light-years.
paper2.lead: Find the time in seconds first. Then turn the seconds into years.
paper2.mi_note: Our answer, marked the SQA way. <var>d</var> = <var>vt</var> (1). 1.58 × 10<sup>17</sup> = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> × <var>t</var>, so <var>t</var> = 5.27 × 10<sup>8</sup> s (1). <var>t</var> = 5.27 × 10<sup>8</sup> ÷ (365.25 × 24 × 60 × 60) = 16.7 years, so 17 light-years (1).

paper2.ref: Our question: metres to light-years (not from an exam paper)
paper2.text:
Vega is 2.4 × 1017 m from Earth.

Calculate this distance in light-years.
paper2.mi_note: Our answer, marked the SQA way. <var>d</var> = <var>vt</var> (1). 2.4 × 10<sup>17</sup> = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> × <var>t</var>, so <var>t</var> = 8.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> s (1). <var>t</var> = 8.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> ÷ (365.25 × 24 × 60 × 60) = 25.4 years, so 25 light-years (1).
